query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under simultaneous mechanical load and corrosive exposure, high-entropy alloys maintain a dynamically self-renewing, defect-tolerant passivation layer that substantially reduces both localized corrosion and wear by rapidly forming and repairing hard oxide or nitride films at contact sites.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy coupons (e.g., FeCoNiCuAl-based or NbMoTaTi-based compositions) with as-cast or laser-cladded microstructures having high hardness and a reported capacity for passivation.
generation.intervention: Perform tribocorrosion testing in an electrochemical cell that allows in situ AFM or confocal microscopy of the alloy surface, while simultaneously monitoring electrochemical potential/current under controlled loads and abrasive contacts in a chloride-containing solution.
generation.conditions: Typical sliding speeds (e.g., 5–10 cm/s) and normal loads (5–10 N) in 0.6–3.5 wt.% NaCl solutions at room temperature with measurements up to 2 hours of continuous reciprocating contact under controlled electrochemical potential.
generation.structural_mediator: Continuous formation, disruption, and reformation of the passivating surface layer, which is hypothesized to be stable enough to limit mechanical wear and tribochemical reactions in the corrosive environment.
generation.mechanism: Multi-principal element-induced lattice distortions, combined with strong oxide or nitride film formation tendencies, lead to hardened surfaces and robust passivation. Mechanical disruption momentarily exposes the alloy, but correlated rapid re-passivation prevents deeper damage and thus diminishes synergy between wear and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a stainless steel baseline, the high-entropy alloy will exhibit at least 20–40% lower wear volume loss, a lower friction coefficient, and up to an order of magnitude lower corrosion current density under combined wear–corrosion conditions. In situ imaging will show repetitive disruption and rapid re-growth of a stable passive layer that effectively confines degradation to shallow, sporadic sites.
generation.baseline: A reference stainless steel coupon tested under identical tribocorrosion conditions is expected to suffer accelerated synergy (higher total wear loss, more pitting, and higher corrosion current density) as the destroyed passive film is slower to heal.
generation.boundary: Under more extreme conditions (e.g., very high normal loads or extremely acidic or high-chloride environments), passivation kinetics may not keep pace with mechanical damage, reducing the protective effect for the high-entropy alloy.
generation.uncertainty: It remains unclear how composition variations (e.g., adjustments in minor alloying elements) might change passivation dynamics; thus the proposed mechanism might not hold for all compositions or loading rates.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the tribocorrosion responses of the high-entropy alloy and a control stainless steel in an electrochemical wear cell with real-time imaging. Intentionally introduce repeated mechanical and chemical perturbations to test the speed and resilience of the protective film’s reformation.
measurements: In situ AFM or confocal imaging of surface film dynamics
Open-circuit potential and corrosion current density paths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy exhibits no evidence of rapid re-passivation (i.e., no visible film reformation upon mechanical disruption) and does not show significantly reduced wear–corrosion synergy relative to stainless steel, then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. At lower content (x = 0.5), B enhances the stability of the passive film and thereby improves corrosion resistance. In contrast

Among corrosive environments, Cl− is one of the most aggressive anions which can cause electrochemical corrosion and the resultant failures of alloys, and the increase in Cl− concentration will further deteriorate the passive film in many conventional alloys. Here, we report single-phase Nb25Mo25Ta25Ti20W5Cx (x = 0.1, 0.3, 0.8 at.%) refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with excellent corrosion resistance in high-concentration NaCl solutions. According to potentiodynamic polarization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, corroded morphology and the current–time results, the RHEAs demonstrate even better corrosion resistance with the increase in NaCl concentration to 23.5 wt.%, significantly superior to 304 L stainless steel. Typically, the corrosion current density (icorr) and over-passivation potential (Et) reached the lowest and highest value, respectively, in the 23.5 wt.% NaCl solution, and the icorr (2.36 × 10−7 A/cm2) of Nb25Mo25Ta25Ti20W5C0.1 alloy is nearly two orders lower than that of 304 L stainless steel (1.75 × 10−5 A/cm2). Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. However, the strong HEA films mentioned above suffer from low ductility in general. How to balance the strength and ductility of amorphous HEA films is important for their applications in the field of flexible microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials. In addition, seeking a high-performance HEA film with low density and corrosion resistance is of great significance for their applications in extreme conditions. In these cases, it is crucial to develop a high hardness, high strength–ductility synergy, and excellent corrosion resistance of amorphous lightweight high entropy alloy film. In this work, the lightweight AlTiVNb HEA film was prepared by magnetron sputtering, and the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance were investigated.

decision.trend: Early work on refractory high-entropy alloys (e.g., CrMoNbWV) established impressive wear resistance and corrosion protection via dense, hard microstructures combined with passivating scales. Subsequent research on FeCoNiCuAl-based compositions further demonstrated that microstructural refinement and controlled phase formation improved both wear and corrosion performance. However, while these studies showed that certain processing routes and compositional tweaks can boost surface hardness and corrosion resistance, they did not pinpoint a unifying mechanistic explanation for how these alloys can resist wear–corrosion synergy in severe environments.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether a dynamically protective surface film or a more fundamental short-range structural feature is primarily responsible for the remarkable synergy of wear and corrosion resistance in high-entropy alloys, and under what conditions such a mechanism might break down.
decision.lever: Perform tribocorrosion testing in an electrochemical cell that allows real-time surface imaging (e.g., in situ AFM or confocal microscopy) and simultaneous electrochemical monitoring, targeting formation and breakdown of surface films under controlled loads, sliding speeds, and aggressive corrosive media (e.g., chloride solutions).
decision.why: Prior studies suggest that both high hardness and stable passivation layers contribute to synergy in wear–corrosion resistance, but the exact mechanism of protective film formation and its mechanical integrity under repeated loading remains unclear. An in situ approach can directly track film evolution, capture dynamic wear–corrosion behavior, and identify critical conditions where protective layers fail—ultimately shedding light on the fundamental processes governing simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance.
